title: Experimental Drug Force-Feeds Cancer Cells Sugar Until They Self-Destruct
excerpt: A University of Texas team developed a first-in-class molecule that overactivates a key metabolic enzyme, turning tumors' glucose addiction into a fatal weakness.
body:
• Researchers developed a first-in-class drug that overactivates a key enzyme in cancer cells, forcing them to metabolize glucose so rapidly that their internal chemistry collapses.
  • The electrophile-drug conjugate (EDC) selectively targets PFKL, a glycolytic enzyme, delivering a toxic payload only to cells with high metabolic activity.
  • The approach works both in cell cultures and in animal models, and introduces EDCs as a new drug-delivery mechanism analogous to antibody-drug conjugates.
  • The study exploits the Warburg effect — cancer cells' well-known addiction to glucose — turning a survival strategy into a fatal vulnerability.

A research team at the University of Texas at Austin has developed an experimental cancer drug that essentially force-feeds tumors sugar until they self-destruct. The approach, detailed in a preprint published on the bioRxiv server, flips one of cancer's most fundamental survival mechanisms on its head.

Turning the Warburg Effect Against Cancer

Cancer cells are famously greedy for glucose. The phenomenon, known as the Warburg effect, describes how tumors rely on rapid glucose metabolism — glycolysis — even when oxygen is plentiful. For decades, researchers have tried to exploit this dependence by starving tumors of sugar or blocking the enzymes involved. The Texas team took the opposite approach: they cranked the metabolic machinery into overdrive.

The drug is built around a small molecule that locks onto phosphofructokinase-1 liver type (PFKL), a gatekeeper enzyme in the glycolytic pathway. By covalently modifying a specific site on PFKL — amino acid K677 in its allosteric effector pocket — the molecule forces the enzyme into a permanently active state. Glucose is pushed through glycolysis at an unsustainable rate, destabilizing the cell's metabolic balance.

A New Drug Delivery Mechanism

What makes the approach especially novel is its delivery system. The researchers call it an electrophile-drug conjugate, or EDC. Like antibody-drug conjugates — a well-established class of cancer therapies — EDCs carry a cytotoxic payload. But instead of relying on antibodies to reach cancer cells from outside, EDCs use covalent chemistry to bind selectively to an intracellular protein target.

"We introduce EDCs as a new delivery mechanism analogous to antibody-drug conjugates but differentiated by selective covalent targeting of intracellular proteins."

— Study authors, University of Texas at Austin

The selectivity is striking. Across the entire proteome, the drug modifies only the K677 site on PFKL, minimizing off-target effects. In both cell cultures and animal models, the EDC suppressed tumor growth while leaving normal cells largely unharmed, according to the researchers.

Why It Matters

Glycolysis-targeting drugs have been a grail in oncology for years, but past efforts have stumbled over the metabolic heterogeneity of tumors — not all cancer cells rely on glucose equally, and resistance develops quickly. By activating rather than inhibiting a metabolic enzyme, the EDC sidesteps some of those barriers. Cells that depend most heavily on glycolysis are the most vulnerable to the metabolic overload.

The research was led by Ku-Lung Hsu's group in the Department of Chemistry at UT Austin, with contributions from the University of Washington. Funding came from multiple NIH grants, including support from the National Cancer Institute and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

What Comes Next

The study remains a preprint and has not yet undergone peer review. The drug has so far been tested only in preclinical settings — cell lines and animal models. Clinical trials in humans are likely years away, and the leap from laboratory results to effective cancer treatment is notoriously difficult. Still, the concept of weaponizing cancer's own metabolic appetite represents a fundamentally different therapeutic strategy, one that could open a new front in the long effort to target the Warburg effect.
